title: Respiratory Embryology
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the lower respiratory tract from a small outgrowth of the foregut in week 4 to the alveolar lung of early childhood. It explains which germ layer builds each tissue, how the trachea separates from the esophagus, how the airway tree and its capillaries mature in stages, and when type II pneumocytes make enough surfactant for air breathing. Board questions usually give a newborn in respiratory distress and ask for the developmental step that failed: septation in tracheoesophageal fistula, surfactant production in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, or lung growth in pulmonary hypoplasia. Knowing the timeline and the mechanism behind each stage lets you predict the finding at birth.
prerequisites: Trilaminar disc and germ layers: endoderm, splanchnic and somatic mesoderm
Folding of the embryo and formation of the primitive gut tube

Alveolar structure: type I and type II pneumocytes, blood-air barrier

connections.how: The lung bud and esophagus come from the same foregut tube, so septation defects join the airway to the gut.
Failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to close lets bowel enter the chest and compress the growing lung.
Fetal urine supplies most amniotic fluid in later pregnancy, so absent or obstructed kidneys starve the lungs of the fluid they need to grow.

connections.to: Respiratory mechanics and gas exchange (PU chapters)
connections.how: Surfactant, compliance, and shunt explain why an immature lung fails once the infant must breathe air.
A small or hypoxic pulmonary vascular bed keeps pulmonary resistance high after birth and drives right-to-left shunting through fetal channels.

A lipoprotein mixture, mostly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, that lowers surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface.
The ratio of these two phospholipids in amniotic fluid, used as an index of fetal lung maturity.

An abnormally small volume of amniotic fluid for gestational age.

sections.title: The lung bud and the germ layer origins of the respiratory tract

blocks.text: In week 4 the respiratory diverticulum, or lung bud, grows out of the ventral wall of the foregut just caudal to the pharynx. Its position is set by signals from the surrounding mesoderm: retinoic acid from that mesoderm induces the transcription factor TBX4 in the overlying endoderm, which marks the site where the bud forms. At first the bud opens freely into the foregut; it is separated from the esophagus by the septation described in the next section and keeps one permanent connection with the pharynx, the laryngeal inlet.

Because the bud is an outpouching of endoderm, every surface that air touches, from the larynx to the alveolus, is endodermal. Endoderm forms the airway lining epithelium, the submucosal glands, and both type I and type II pneumocytes. The bud grows into the splanchnic mesoderm that surrounds the foregut, and that mesoderm forms everything in the wall: cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue, blood vessels, and the visceral pleura covering the lung. The parietal pleura comes from somatic mesoderm lining the body wall. The larynx is the exception in the wall: its cartilages and muscles come from the mesenchyme of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6, so they are supplied by the nerves of those arches, the superior laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches of the vagus nerve.

blocks.title: Germ layer origins of the respiratory tract
rows: Epithelium of larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli (type I and II pneumocytes); airway glands
Cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue, and vessels of the trachea and lungs; visceral pleura
Thyroid cartilage and cricothyroid muscle; superior laryngeal nerve
Cricoid and arytenoid cartilages and the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles; recurrent laryngeal nerve
blocks.caption: Lining and glands are endodermal; the supporting wall is mesodermal. Arch assignments of the smaller laryngeal cartilages differ slightly between texts.

blocks.text: Branching is a conversation between the two layers. The mesenchyme secretes signals such as fibroblast growth factor 10 (FGF10) that tell the endodermal tip where to grow and divide, and endoderm grafted next to tracheal mesenchyme fails to branch. Early in week 5 the bud splits into right and left bronchial buds. The right forms three secondary (lobar) bronchi and the left forms two, which fixes three lobes on the right and two on the left. Each lobar bronchus then gives tertiary (segmental) bronchi, about ten on the right and eight to ten on the left, which define the bronchopulmonary segments. As the lungs enlarge they grow laterally into the pericardioperitoneal canals, which become the pleural cavities.

Errors in budding explain several anomalies. An abnormal extra bud from the foregut or airway can pinch off as a bronchogenic cyst, usually in the mediastinum near the carina, lined by respiratory epithelium and containing cartilage and smooth muscle because both layers took part. Abnormal division of the bronchial tree produces accessory lobes or atypical segments, which can mimic disease on imaging.

sections.title: Tracheoesophageal septation and esophageal atresia with fistula

blocks.text: When the lung bud first appears, the future trachea and esophagus share one lumen. Longitudinal tracheoesophageal ridges grow in from each side of the foregut and fuse in the midline, forming the tracheoesophageal septum. The septum divides the foregut into a ventral laryngotracheal tube and a dorsal esophagus, which is why the trachea lies anterior to the esophagus throughout the neck and upper thorax. Septation stops at the larynx, where the airway keeps its opening into the pharynx.

If the septum deviates posteriorly or the ridges fail to fuse completely, a channel between the airway and the gut persists, and the esophagus often fails to remain continuous. Fistula and atresia therefore usually occur together. Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula occurs in about 1 in 3,000 to 4,500 births and is part of the VACTERL association (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies) in a substantial minority of cases, so finding one anomaly should prompt a search for the others.

blocks.title: Types of esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula
cols: Key findings explained by the anatomy
rows: Blind upper esophageal pouch; lower esophagus joins trachea (distal fistula)
Polyhydramnios, drooling, choking and cyanosis with first feed, tube coils in pouch, gas-filled stomach and bowel
Marked polyhydramnios, drooling, gasless abdomen because no air can reach the stomach
Feeds pass normally, so diagnosis is delayed; recurrent aspiration pneumonia and coughing with feeds
Proximal fistula, or fistulas to both segments
Immediate aspiration of feeds from the upper pouch into the airway
blocks.caption: Frequencies are approximate and vary between series; the distal fistula type is consistently the most common.

blocks.title: How the common type produces its findings
steps: Tracheoesophageal septum forms abnormally
Upper esophagus ends blindly; lower esophagus opens into trachea
Fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid: polyhydramnios
Newborn cannot clear saliva: drooling, choking
Feeds overflow the pouch into the larynx: cough, cyanosis
Air enters stomach through the fistula: gastric distension
Gastric acid refluxes up the fistula: chemical pneumonitis
blocks.caption: Each sign follows from the blind upper pouch or from the open path between trachea and lower esophagus.

blocks.text: Polyhydramnios is the prenatal clue because the fetus normally swallows large volumes of amniotic fluid and absorbs it in the intestine; a blind pouch blocks that route while urine output continues. The excess is greatest without a distal fistula, since a fistula lets some fluid reach the gut through the trachea. After birth, a feeding tube that will not pass into the stomach and instead coils in the upper pouch on a radiograph confirms the atresia, and gas below the diaphragm shows that a distal fistula exists. The distal fistula also harms the lungs from below: a crying infant pumps air into the stomach, distension splints the diaphragm, and acid gastric content can reflux into the trachea.

blocks.predict: Two newborns have esophageal atresia. One has a distended, gas-filled abdomen on radiograph; the other has no gas below the diaphragm. Which anatomy does each have?
blocks.explain: Air reaches the stomach only through a fistula from the trachea to the lower esophagus, so a gas-filled abdomen means a distal fistula (the common type). A gasless abdomen means atresia without a distal fistula.

sections.title: Stages of lung development and the limit of viability

blocks.text: After the embryonic period lays down the lung bud and the lobar and segmental bronchi, the lung matures through four overlapping stages. Each stage adds a structure that the next one needs. The key to timing questions is that gas exchange requires two things side by side: an airspace with thin epithelium and a capillary pressed against it.

blocks.title: Stages of lung development
rows: Lung bud, main, lobar, and segmental bronchi
Branching down to terminal bronchioles; cartilage, glands, and smooth muscle appear
Respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts; capillaries invade and approach thinning epithelium; first type I and II cells
Becomes possible only near the end, about weeks 24 to 26
Thin-walled terminal sacs (primitive alveoli) lined by type I and II cells; capillaries bulge into them
Mature alveoli with thin septa; alveolar number rises steeply after birth
blocks.caption: Stages overlap because branching proceeds at different rates in different regions; boundaries are approximate.

blocks.text: In the pseudoglandular stage the lung looks like a gland: blind epithelial tubes in thick mesenchyme. By about week 16 all conducting airways down to the terminal bronchioles exist, so the airway branching pattern is set before mid-gestation. No breathing is possible at this stage regardless of support, because there are no respiratory bronchioles and the capillaries lie far from the epithelium.

The canalicular stage is named for the vascular canals that grow into the mesenchyme. Terminal bronchioles divide into respiratory bronchioles, which give alveolar ducts, the lumens widen, the epithelium flattens, and capillaries move up against it. Near the end of this stage, at about weeks 24 to 26, enough thin interface exists for an infant to exchange gas with intensive support. That is why the limit of viability falls here: before this point the problem is structural and cannot be overcome, whereas after it the main limits are surfactant and barrier thickness, which improve week by week.

In the saccular stage the airspaces become terminal sacs, type I cells thin to form a barrier only a fraction of a micrometer thick, and type II cells increase. The alveolar stage adds true alveoli by secondary septation, in which new walls grow out from the sac walls and subdivide them. Most adult alveoli form after birth, mainly in the first two to three years, which gives an injured or premature lung some capacity to catch up. Before birth the airspaces are filled mainly with fluid secreted by the airway epithelium rather than with amniotic fluid, and fetal breathing movements move this fluid and stretch the lung.

blocks.title: Predicting outcome from gestational age
blocks.text: Infant A is born at 22 weeks; infant B at 27 weeks. At 22 weeks the lung is early in the canalicular stage: respiratory bronchioles are only beginning to form and most capillaries are still separated from the airspaces by thick mesenchyme, so even full support delivers little oxygen to blood. At 27 weeks the lung is entering the saccular stage: terminal sacs and close capillaries exist, so gas exchange is structurally possible, but type II cells are few and surfactant is far below the level reached near week 35. Infant B can survive but will very likely develop neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, while infant A faces a structural barrier rather than a surfactant problem.

sections.title: Surfactant production and fetal lung maturity

blocks.text: Surfactant is about 90% lipid and 10% protein. Its main lipid is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), a lecithin; phosphatidylglycerol and surfactant proteins A, B, C, and D complete the mixture. Type II pneumocytes synthesize it, store it in lamellar bodies, and secrete it by exocytosis onto the alveolar lining fluid. SP-B and SP-C help spread the lipid into a film; SP-A and SP-D are collectins that bind microbes and aid innate defense.

By the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r), the pressure that tends to collapse an alveolus rises as its radius falls. Surfactant lowers surface tension, and it lowers it most in small alveoli, where the film is compressed and more concentrated. This keeps small alveoli from emptying into large ones, raises compliance, and reduces the force that would otherwise draw fluid from capillaries into the airspaces.

Type II cells appear in the canalicular stage and begin secreting surfactant in the second trimester, but output rises steeply only late in gestation and becomes adequate at about week 35. Fetal cortisol, which surges near term, induces the enzymes of phospholipid synthesis and the surfactant proteins; thyroid hormone also accelerates maturation. Insulin opposes the glucocorticoid effect, so in maternal diabetes fetal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperinsulinemia and delayed maturation. Male sex and cesarean delivery without labor (less stress cortisol and catecholamine) also raise risk.

Fetal lung fluid flows up the trachea into the amniotic fluid, carrying surfactant with it, so amniotic fluid samples the lung. Sphingomyelin stays roughly constant through late gestation while lecithin rises sharply after about weeks 32 to 34. An L/S ratio above 2 indicates mature lungs and a low risk of respiratory distress; a ratio below about 1.5 indicates high risk. Diabetic pregnancy is the classic exception, because distress can occur despite a ratio above 2; the appearance of phosphatidylglycerol, a late component of mature surfactant, is more reliable there. Blood or meconium in the sample can distort the ratio.

blocks.title: From surfactant deficiency to neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
steps: Birth before type II cells make enough surfactant
High surface tension in small alveoli
Alveoli collapse at end expiration: diffuse atelectasis
Low compliance raises work of breathing: retractions, grunting
Perfused, unventilated alveoli act as shunt: hypoxemia
Epithelial and endothelial injury leaks protein: hyaline membranes
blocks.caption: Collapse, shunt, and protein leak explain the clinical and pathologic findings.

blocks.title: Self-sustaining injury in respiratory distress syndrome
steps: Surfactant deficiency causes atelectasis
Shunt produces hypoxemia and acidosis
Hypoxia and acidosis impair type II cell surfactant synthesis
Hypoxic vasoconstriction raises pulmonary resistance
Right-to-left shunting through ductus and foramen ovale worsens hypoxemia
blocks.caption: Each step deepens the deficit that started the loop.

blocks.text: Grunting is expiration against a partly closed glottis, which holds pressure in the airways and keeps alveoli open. The radiograph shows diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms, because air-filled bronchi stand out against collapsed alveoli. Hyaline membranes, made of fibrin and necrotic epithelial debris, line the alveolar ducts and further thicken the barrier.

blocks.predict: A 36-week fetus of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes has an amniotic L/S ratio of 2.2 and no phosphatidylglycerol. Is the lung safely mature?
blocks.explain: Not reliably. Fetal hyperinsulinemia blunts the glucocorticoid drive on type II cells, so the surfactant may be functionally immature despite a ratio above 2. Absent phosphatidylglycerol supports that concern.

sections.title: Pulmonary hypoplasia from oligohydramnios and diaphragmatic hernia

blocks.text: Normal lung growth depends on mechanical stretch. The fetal airway epithelium secretes fluid by active chloride transport, and the larynx and upper airway resist its outflow, so the lung stays distended at a pressure slightly above that of the amniotic cavity. Fetal breathing movements, which need an intact diaphragm and phrenic nerve, add cyclic stretch. Three conditions must therefore be met: fluid held in the airways, adequate room in the chest, and fetal breathing. Loss of any one, especially during the pseudoglandular and canalicular stages, leaves a lung with fewer airway generations, fewer alveoli, and a smaller vascular bed.

From the second trimester on, fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid. In bilateral renal agenesis there is almost no urine, so oligohydramnios develops. The uterus then compresses the fetal chest, and the lost external fluid pressure lets lung fluid drain out, removing the distending force. The resulting Potter sequence combines pulmonary hypoplasia with compression features: flattened nose, low-set ears, receding chin, and limb positioning deformities such as clubfeet. Urinary tract obstruction (posterior urethral valves in males), autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, and prolonged rupture of membranes cause the same lung outcome by the same route.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia results from failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to close the pleuroperitoneal canal, which normally happens around week 7. The defect is usually posterolateral (Bochdalek) and about 85% are left-sided, because the left canal is larger and closes later and the liver shields the right. When the midgut returns from the umbilical cord at about week 10, bowel can pass into the chest during the pseudoglandular stage. The ipsilateral lung is most affected, but mediastinal shift compresses the other lung too, so both are often hypoplastic.

blocks.title: Two routes to pulmonary hypoplasia
steps: Renal agenesis or obstruction, or a diaphragmatic defect
Oligohydramnios compresses chest, or bowel fills hemithorax
Lung fluid and stretch lost during branching
Fewer airways, alveoli, and pulmonary arteries
Small gas exchange area and high vascular resistance at birth
blocks.caption: Both causes converge on reduced stretch while the airway tree is forming.

blocks.text: At birth the small lung cannot exchange enough gas, and the pulmonary arteries are few and abnormally muscular far into the periphery, so pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall. Blood shunts right to left through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn), causing profound hypoxemia, often with higher oxygen saturation in the right arm than in the legs. Stiff, small lungs also rupture easily, giving pneumothorax. In diaphragmatic hernia the abdomen is scaphoid because its contents are in the chest, bowel sounds may be heard over the hemithorax, and heart sounds shift away from the hernia, usually to the right.

blocks.title: Causes of pulmonary hypoplasia
rows: Bilateral renal agenesis, posterior urethral valves, prolonged membrane rupture
External compression and loss of distending lung fluid
Too little space in the chest
Diaphragmatic hernia, large pleural effusion, small bony thorax
Direct compression of the growing lung
Severe neuromuscular disease, phrenic nerve injury
blocks.caption: Any cause that removes stretch during branching reduces lung growth.

blocks.predict: Why does polyhydramnios accompany esophageal atresia, while oligohydramnios accompanies renal agenesis, and which of the two causes pulmonary hypoplasia?
blocks.explain: Atresia blocks fetal swallowing, which removes fluid, so fluid accumulates; agenesis removes urine, the main fluid source, so fluid falls. Only oligohydramnios compresses the chest and drains lung fluid, so only renal agenesis causes hypoplasia.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology set the stage. The lung is a foregut derivative, so its anomalies cluster with gut, cardiac, renal, and vertebral defects, and the timing of the diaphragm, the return of the midgut, and the onset of fetal urine production all intersect with the pseudoglandular and canalicular stages. Biochemistry explains maturity: surfactant synthesis is a glucocorticoid-regulated lipid pathway opposed by insulin, which links maternal diabetes to delayed lung maturity. Immunology enters through SP-A and SP-D, which act as collectins, and through the infection risk of a lung that aspirates gastric content through a fistula.

Physiology and pathology then explain the newborn. Surface tension, compliance, and shunt account for respiratory distress syndrome, while a small vascular bed accounts for the pulmonary hypertension of hypoplasia. The limits are real: gestational age boundaries are approximate, the L/S ratio can mislead in diabetic pregnancy, and several conditions can coexist, so the newborn's findings are read against the whole developmental history.

summary: The lung bud arises from ventral foregut endoderm in week 4; endoderm forms all airway and alveolar epithelium and glands, while splanchnic mesoderm forms cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue, vessels, and visceral pleura.
Laryngeal cartilages and muscles come from pharyngeal arches 4 and 6, supplied by the superior and recurrent laryngeal branches of the vagus nerve.
Fusion of the tracheoesophageal ridges forms the septum that places the trachea anterior to the esophagus; faulty septation gives esophageal atresia with fistula.
The most common type is a blind upper pouch with a distal fistula: polyhydramnios, drooling, choking with feeds, a coiled tube, and a gas-filled stomach.
Branching to terminal bronchioles is complete by about week 16; the canalicular stage adds respiratory bronchioles and close capillaries, so survival first becomes possible near weeks 24 to 26.
Most alveoli form after birth, and alveolarization continues into childhood.
Type II pneumocytes begin surfactant secretion in the second trimester, reaching adequate levels near week 35; cortisol speeds and insulin delays maturation.
An L/S ratio above 2 indicates lung maturity, but phosphatidylglycerol is more reliable in diabetic pregnancy.
Surfactant deficiency causes atelectasis, shunt, low compliance, and hyaline membranes, a loop worsened by hypoxia and acidosis.
Oligohydramnios and diaphragmatic hernia cause pulmonary hypoplasia by removing stretch during branching, leading to respiratory failure and persistent pulmonary hypertension at birth.

verify: Stage boundaries differ between texts (for example pseudoglandular weeks 5 to 16 or 5 to 17; alveolar stage from week 32 or 36 to age 2, 3, or 8); confirm the ranges NABNE uses.
The limit of viability is stated here as weeks 24 to 26 per the competency; current neonatal care reports survival at 22 to 23 weeks, so confirm which figure NABNE expects.
Frequencies of esophageal atresia and fistula types (distal fistula 85 to 90%, isolated atresia 5 to 8%, H-type about 4%) and overall incidence vary among series.
L/S cutoffs (mature above 2, high risk below about 1.5) and the gestational age at which lecithin rises (about weeks 32 to 34) vary slightly by laboratory and source.

Arch assignments of the individual laryngeal cartilages (thyroid from arch 4; cricoid and arytenoid from arch 6) are taught differently in some texts, which assign all laryngeal cartilages jointly to arches 4 and 6.
The classic ridge-fusion model of tracheoesophageal septation is the one tested; recent developmental studies describe the separation differently, so the board model is used here.
Percentage of left-sided diaphragmatic hernias (about 80 to 90%) and the week of pleuroperitoneal closure (about week 6 to 7) differ slightly between sources.
Requested new diagram names for a future revision: lung-stages (timeline of the five stages with viability marked) and tef-types (the four common atresia and fistula configurations).
